newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - New economic era close as UK jobless rate dips.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New economic era close as UK jobless rate dips.

text.p: The British economy could be on the brink of a new era where fast growth and low unemployment are not accompanied by a surge in inflation, the so-called New Paradigm, economists say.

U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has said that supply side and technological improvements may have quickened the sustainable growth rate there, engendering the economic equivalent of nirvana, and analysts say a similar scenario is within Britain's grasp too.

"It is fascinating that whereas unemployment is down to 5.5 percent there is as yet no major sign that pay settlements are starting to pick up," said Ruth Lea, head of the policy unit at the Institute of Directors.
"It does seem as though the economy is able to operate with slightly less spare capacity and not encounter wage inflation. But there's no room for complacency."
"NATURAL" JOBLESS RATE FALLS

Analysts argue that the "natural" jobless total, the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment which is known as the NAIRU, has probably fallen from around eight percent in the 1980s to five or six percent now.
"I think it's quite clear that in the U.S. and the UK the natural rate of unemployment has come down," said SBC- Warburg economist Darren Winder.
"What we are now waiting to see is whether that spreads to the rest of Europe, although clearly they have not undergone the same supply side reforms that we have."

Winder said the New Paradigm was within reach. He forecast unemployment down to 3.5 percent in 1999 but with average earnings growth -- a crucial barometer of inflation pressures -- at no point straying over 5.0 percent for more than a short period of time. By contrast the rate peaked at around 10 percent in the boom of the late 1980s.
Recent data suggested Britain might have already broken out of the old mould of low unemployment which boosts wage claims and in turn fuels inflation.
July unemployment fell to 5.5 percent to a level of 1.55 million, the lowest since September 1980, while June average earnings growth remained at just 4.25 percent.
This combination bodes well for the British authorities, battling to ensure the current mini-boom does not end in yet another bust, sparked by rampant consumer demand.
AUTHORITIES MUST CONTINUE PRE-EMPTIVE MONETARY POLICY
Analysts think the Bank of England's current "stitch in time" approach of regular 1/4 point interest rate rises could help avoid the policy mistakes of the past.

"What matters is that the Bank must stay ahead of the curve to make sure we approach equilibrium on growth and unemployment steadily," said Brian Henry, economics professor at the London Business School and a former official at the Bank of England (central bank) and the International Monetary Fund.

British interest rates have risen in each of the past four months and the Bank of England, which took over conduct of monetary policy in May, has now announced a hiatus while it assesses the impact of the rate increases so far.
"What happened in the late 1980s was that we increased demand too rapidly, we should not let that happen again," Henry said.

Spiralling wages and prices sent inflation to 10.9 percent in the late 1980s, saw official interest rates soar to 15 percent -- more than twice their 7.0 percent level now -- and ended in the longest recession since World War Two.
SUPPLY SIDE REFORMS MAY KEEP PAY CLAIMS LOW

Analysts say that the Conservative Party's deregulation of British industry in the 1980s reduced trades union powers. Easier terms for hiring and firing staff have handed the new Labour government a more flexible workforce, less likely to strike or demand hefty pay rises.

"There's an argument that people are psychologically much more cowed and depressed than they were 10 years ago and are not prepared to stick their necks out and ask for more pay in case they lose their jobs," said Nick Isles, director of development at the Employment Policy Institute.
But he said there were potential clouds on the horizon with the buoyant service sector already near full capacity. "The crucial time will be new pay round in the autumn."

The recent increases in interest rates, which have already boosted the headline inflation rate to 3.3 percent in July from 2.9 in June by making mortgage costs dearer, could provoke demands for higher wages to compensate.
The hawkish Bank of England is concerned that continued labour market tightening could pose an inflation threat but some analysts argue there is little to worry about yet.

"The Bank needs to take the same approach as the (U.S.) Federal Reserve -- suck it and see," said Yamaichi Chief Economist John Shepperd. He said the bank should monitor the economy for warning signs but with an open mind.
"We have a similar structural position to the U.S. and it looks as though we're going down a similar path."
